extracted.intended_audience: researchers, statisticians, and practitioners who measure inter-rater agreement (students and applied researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for computing, interpreting, and critiquing Cohen's kappa as a measure of agreement between two raters classifying categorical data. Covers formulae, examples, confidence intervals, weighted variants, limitations, and related statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and core formula of Cohen's kappa
rubrics_metrics.description: κ ≡ (p_o − p_e) / (1 − p_e), where p_o is the relative observed agreement among raters and p_e is the hypothetical probability of chance agreement (calculated from observed marginals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: p_o is the observed proportionate agreement. p_e is computed using the observed data to calculate the probabilities of each observer randomly selecting each category, using the independence assumption: p_e = (1/N^2) ∑_k n_{k1} n_{k2} (or equivalently ∑_k 7p_{k1}7p_{k2}). If raters are in complete agreement κ = 1; if agreement equals that expected by p_e then κ = 0; κ can be negative when agreement is less than expected by p_e.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation of expected agreement p_e from marginals
rubrics_metrics.description: p_e is the probability of chance agreement calculated from the marginal totals: p_e = ∑_k 7p_{k1}7p_{k2} = (1/N^2) ∑_k n_{k1} n_{k2}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate p_{k1} as n_{k1}/N and p_{k2} as n_{k2}/N. The relation uses the assumption that the ratings of the two raters are independent. This construction is central to kappa and explains why marginal distributions strongly influence kappa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Range and basic interpretation of κ values
rubrics_metrics.description: κ ranges from -1 (complete disagreement) to 1 (complete agreement); κ = 0 corresponds to agreement expected by the chance baseline p_e.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative κ can occur by chance or reflect a tendency for raters to disagree. The numerical value alone needs context (see interpretation guidelines and limitations) because factors such as prevalence and marginal bias influence κ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binary-classification (confusion matrix) formula
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This expression shows Cohen's kappa is equivalent to the Heidke skill score for binary classification. TP, FP, TN, FN denote true positives, false positives, true negatives, and false negatives respectively; use this formula when evaluating binary classifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighted kappa for ordered/graded disagreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Weighted κ allows disagreements to be weighted differently and uses three matrices: observed scores, expected scores, and a weight matrix w_{ij}. The equation: κ = 1 - (∑_{i,j} w_{ij} x_{ij}) / (∑_{i,j} w_{ij} m_{ij}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weight matrix diagonal entries (agreement) are zero; off-diagonal weights indicate seriousness of disagreement (e.g., 1 for adjacent categories, 2 for two-off). When diagonal weights are 0 and all off-diagonal weights are 1, weighted κ reduces to unweighted Cohen's kappa. Useful when categories are ordinal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis testing, standard error, and confidence intervals for κ
rubrics_metrics.description: P-values for κ are rarely reported; standard error SE_κ can be estimated by jackknife, bootstrap, or asymptotic formulae. Confidence interval: CI: κ ± Z_{1-α/2} SE_κ (with Z_{1-α/2}=1.96 for α=5%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although significance testing is possible, a statistically significant but small κ may not indicate practically useful agreement. Use SE and CI methods appropriate for sample size and study design (jackknife/bootstrap for small samples or complex designs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting magnitude: published guidelines (and their limitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common magnitude guidelines: Landis & Koch characterize <0 as no agreement, 0–0.20 slight, 0.21–0.40 fair, 0.41–0.60 moderate, 0.61–0.80 substantial, 0.81–1 almost perfect. Fleiss suggested >0.75 excellent, 0.40–0.75 fair to good, <0.40 poor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These scales are arbitrary and not universally accepted; Landis & Koch supplied no empirical justification and such fixed cutoffs may be misleading. Use context-specific considerations rather than blind thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of prevalence, marginal bias, and number of codes on κ
rubrics_metrics.description: Kappa values are affected by prevalence (distribution of codes), bias (differences in marginal probabilities between raters), and the number of categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kappas are higher when codes are equiprobable; bias (unequal marginals) alters kappa, with bias effects larger when κ is small. Increasing number of codes tends to increase κ for fallible observers (simulation evidence). Therefore compare κ values only when prevalence and marginals are similar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kappa maximum (κ_max) given unequal marginals
rubrics_metrics.description: κ_max = (P_max − P_exp) / (1 − P_exp), where P_exp = ∑_i P_{i+} P_{+i} and P_max = ∑_i min(P_{i+}, P_{+i}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: κ reaches 1 only when both observers distribute codes identically (row and column sums identical). Computing κ_max helps interpret an observed κ when marginals are unequal by showing the maximum achievable κ given the marginals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation: baseline agreement and the distinction between quantity and allocation disagreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Kappa's baseline is the agreement expected due to the marginal totals of the contingency table, not a general notion of chance. κ = 0 when observed allocation is apparently random relative to those marginals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For many applications reporting quantity disagreement (differences in marginal totals) and allocation disagreement (off-diagonal allocations) separately is more informative than a single κ. Examples in the article show cases where κ is near zero or negative despite different patterns of quantity/allocation disagreement, demonstrating that κ can obscure useful information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation: poor behavior with rare categories (conservative / underestimation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kappa can be unreliable for measuring agreement on rare categories because it tends to underestimate agreement on the rare category; thus κ is considered overly conservative in such situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When diagnosing rare conditions or categories with very low prevalence, supplement κ with category-specific agreement measures or report marginal and per-class agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critiques of the chance-adjustment assumption and unbalanced data
rubrics_metrics.description: Some researchers contest that kappa 'takes into account' chance agreement because doing so would require an explicit model of how chance affects decisions; the usual chance adjustment implicitly assumes raters guess when uncertain. Works have shown kappa can give wrong conclusions for unbalanced data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious interpreting κ when the guessing/independence model is unrealistic or when data are highly unbalanced. Consider alternative measures or explicit probabilistic models of rater behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Related/alternative statistics to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternatives and related measures include Scott's pi (differs in p_e calculation), Fleiss' kappa (multi-rater generalization of Scott's pi), intraclass correlation, Informedness/Youden's J (directional version for supervised learning), and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) which some argue is more informative for binary classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose an alternative when appropriate: use Fleiss' kappa for >2 raters, intraclass correlation for continuous scores, Youden's J or MCC for classification performance in ML. Compare how each computes chance/expected agreement before selecting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical computation and interpretability cautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Kappa is a ratio and may be undefined if the denominator (1 − p_e) is zero; the ratio form hides numerator and denominator information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report components p_o and p_e (or quantity and allocation disagreement) alongside κ. Use computational tools that return SE and CI; consider reporting contingency table summaries so readers can judge marginal effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worked examples and illustrative pitfalls
rubrics_metrics.description: The article provides a simple 2-rater example (50 items, A/B readers, Yes/No counts) showing p_o = 0.7, p_e = 0.5, κ = 0.4; and contrasting cases with same percent agreement (60/100) but different marginals yielding different κ values (0.1304 vs 0.2593).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples to demonstrate how identical percent agreement can give quite different κ because p_e differs; use such illustrations when teaching or defending choice of agreement metric.
